title: TLS & HTTPS Internals
tagline: Inside the TLS 1.3 handshake: certificates, PKI trust chains, cipher suite negotiation, and how forward secrecy is achieved on every HTTPS connection.

sections.content:
Every time your browser shows a padlock icon, something remarkable has happened in milliseconds: two strangers — your laptop and a server thousands of kilometres away — have negotiated a shared secret over a completely public network, verified each other's identities using a global web of cryptographic trust, and agreed on how to encrypt everything they say next. No one listening on the wire can read a single byte of your data. No impersonator can fake the server's identity without possessing a private key that never leaves the server. This is **TLS — Transport Layer Security**.

TLS sits between TCP and HTTP in the networking stack. TCP delivers bytes reliably across the internet. HTTP structures those bytes into requests and responses. TLS sits in between and guarantees three security properties: **confidentiality** (only sender and recipient can read the data), **integrity** (any tampering is detected and the connection aborted), and **authentication** (you are provably talking to the real server, not an impersonator). HTTPS is simply HTTP running over a TLS-protected TCP connection.

TLS 1.3 — standardised in RFC 8446 in August 2018 — was a landmark redesign. It shrunk the handshake from 2 round trips to 1, encrypted more of the handshake itself (including the server's certificate), removed every weak and legacy cipher suite, and made **forward secrecy** mandatory rather than optional. Understanding its internals is not academic curiosity: it determines whether your server is vulnerable to downgrade attacks, whether past traffic is safe if your private key is stolen, and why certificate expiry causes a hard outage rather than a gentle warning.

This chapter builds TLS from its cryptographic primitives up: symmetric encryption, asymmetric cryptography, the Diffie-Hellman key exchange, X.509 certificates, the PKI trust hierarchy, and finally how TLS 1.3 combines all of them into a single, beautifully orchestrated handshake.

sections.title: Passport Control, a Sealed Envelope, and Dice Rolls
sections.content:
Imagine arriving at a foreign border crossing where you have never been before. The border officer (the server) shows you their **government-issued passport** — the TLS certificate. You examine it: the photo matches, the official government stamp (the Certificate Authority's cryptographic signature) is genuine, and the issuing government is one you trust (a root CA in your browser's trust store). You are now confident you are talking to the real official, not an impostor.

Next comes the key exchange. You and the officer each secretly roll a set of dice in a black box. You each see only your own dice and the other person's *result* — not the rolls themselves. Yet through mathematical magic (the **Diffie-Hellman** algorithm), you can both combine your private rolls with the other's public result to arrive at the same shared secret number. Anyone watching the border crossing sees the results but cannot compute the shared secret without knowing one of the private rolls.

From that shared number, you independently derive the same cipher key — your **session key**. You lock all further conversation in a box with that key. Here is the crucial part: you then **throw away the dice**. Even if an adversary somehow stole the officer's master credentials months later, they could not replay your conversation, because the session key was derived from ephemeral dice rolls that no longer exist. This is **forward secrecy**, and it is why TLS 1.3 mandates it.

sections.title: The Two Cryptographic Worlds TLS Bridges
sections.content:
TLS uses two fundamentally different kinds of cryptography, each good at something the other is not.

**Symmetric encryption** uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt. It is extremely fast — modern CPUs have hardware instructions for AES that can encrypt gigabytes per second. The problem: how do two strangers agree on a shared key without an eavesdropper learning it?

**Asymmetric (public-key) cryptography** uses a mathematically linked key pair: a **public key** anyone can have, and a **private key** that never leaves the owner. Messages encrypted with the public key can only be decrypted with the private key. Conversely, a message signed with the private key can be verified with the public key. Asymmetric operations are thousands of times slower than symmetric ones, so they are only used during the handshake — not for bulk data.

TLS's elegant solution: use **asymmetric cryptography during the handshake** to securely agree on a shared secret, then use **symmetric encryption for all application data**. The handshake's job is to bootstrap trust and key material. Once the session keys are derived, TLS switches to a fast authenticated encryption scheme like `AES-256-GCM` or `ChaCha20-Poly1305`.

**AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data)** is the modern standard. AES-GCM, for example, simultaneously encrypts data and computes an authentication tag. The recipient checks the tag before decrypting — if any bit was altered in transit, the tag check fails and the connection is torn down. This binds confidentiality and integrity into a single, efficient operation, which is why TLS 1.3 only allows AEAD cipher suites.

sections.title: The Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange: How Strangers Share a Secret
sections.content:
The **Diffie-Hellman (DH) key exchange**, invented by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman in 1976, solves the fundamental problem of exchanging a secret over a public channel. TLS 1.3 uses its elliptic-curve variant, **ECDHE** (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral).

The underlying idea, stripped to its essence, uses the **discrete logarithm problem**: raising a number to a power modulo a prime is easy to compute, but reversing it (finding the exponent given the result) is computationally infeasible for large numbers. Elliptic curves achieve the same property with smaller key sizes — a 256-bit ECDH key provides security comparable to a 3072-bit classical DH key.

Here is how it works in TLS 1.3:
1. Both client and server agree on an **elliptic curve** (e.g., `X25519`, `P-256`). The client announces which curves it supports in `ClientHello`; the server picks one.
2. The **client** generates an ephemeral private key `a` (a random 256-bit integer) and computes the corresponding public key `A = a * G` where `G` is the curve's base point. The client sends `A` in the `key_share` extension of `ClientHello`.
3. The **server** generates its own ephemeral private key `b` and public key `B = b * G`. The server sends `B` in `ServerHello`.
4. The **client** computes the shared secret: `S = a * B = a * (b * G)`.
5. The **server** computes the same: `S = b * A = b * (a * G)`.
6. Both arrive at the same point `S` on the curve. An eavesdropper sees `A` and `B` but cannot compute `S` without either `a` or `b`.

From `S`, both sides run a **Key Derivation Function (HKDF)** to produce the actual session keys (different keys for client-to-server and server-to-client, and separate keys for the handshake phase vs. the application data phase).

The **E** in ECDHE stands for **Ephemeral**: both `a` and `b` are generated fresh for every handshake and discarded immediately after key derivation. This is the source of forward secrecy — even if an attacker records all encrypted traffic and later steals the server's long-term private key (from the certificate), they cannot recompute `a` or `b`, so they cannot derive the session keys.

sections.title: X.509 Certificates: Binding a Public Key to an Identity
sections.content:
A **TLS certificate** is an X.509 document that answers a critical question: 'Whose public key is this?' Without certificates, the Diffie-Hellman exchange is vulnerable to a **man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack** — an attacker intercepts both sides and performs two separate ECDHE exchanges, impersonating the server to the client and vice versa. The client would happily derive a session key with the attacker, not the real server.

Certificates prevent this by digitally binding a public key to an identity (a domain name). A certificate contains:
- **Subject**: Who does this certificate belong to? Includes `CN` (Common Name) and more importantly the **Subject Alternative Names (SANs)** extension listing every domain and IP the cert is valid for.
- **Public key**: The subject's public key (used for signature verification in `CertificateVerify`).
- **Validity period**: `notBefore` and `notAfter` timestamps. Most publicly issued certificates expire after 90 days (Let's Encrypt) to one year.
- **Issuer**: Which Certificate Authority signed this certificate?
- **Signature**: The CA's digital signature over all the above fields, made with the CA's private key.
- **Serial number** and **extensions**: Including `keyUsage`, `extendedKeyUsage`, OCSP responder URL, `Certificate Transparency` (CT) log proof, and more.

**Certificate Verification** proceeds in steps:
1. **Signature chain**: Walk from the leaf certificate to a trusted root. Each certificate's signature is verified using the issuer's public key. If any link breaks, the chain is invalid.
2. **SANs match**: The domain the client is trying to reach must match one of the Subject Alternative Names (wildcards like `*.example.com` match one subdomain level).
3. **Validity period**: The current time must fall between `notBefore` and `notAfter`.
4. **Revocation check**: Has the CA revoked this certificate before it expired? Checked via CRL or OCSP.
5. **Certificate Transparency**: Was the certificate logged in a CT log before issuance? Chrome requires this.

In TLS 1.3, the server sends the `Certificate` message (containing the leaf cert plus any intermediate certs) and a `CertificateVerify` message — a **signature** over the entire handshake transcript using the certificate's private key. This proves the server possesses the private key matching the certificate's public key, closing the MITM gap.

sections.title: The PKI Trust Hierarchy: How Browsers Trust Root CAs
sections.content:
**PKI (Public Key Infrastructure)** is the global system that makes certificate-based authentication work at internet scale. It is built on a chain of trust rooted in a small set of **root Certificate Authorities** whose public keys come pre-installed in your operating system or browser.

Browsers and operating systems ship with roughly 100–150 trusted root CA certificates from major CAs: DigiCert, Sectigo, Let's Encrypt (via ISRG Root), GlobalSign, Entrust, and others. These root CAs are offline — their private keys are stored in hardware security modules (HSMs) in physically secured facilities, used only for signing intermediate CA certificates.

**Intermediate CAs** do the actual work of signing leaf certificates. This architecture serves two purposes: (1) the root CA's private key is kept offline, dramatically reducing its exposure; (2) if an intermediate CA is compromised, browsers can revoke it without touching the root.

**Certificate Authorities issue three types of end-entity certificates** based on how thoroughly they validated the applicant:
- **DV (Domain Validated)**: The CA verifies only that the applicant controls the domain, typically via a DNS TXT record or a file at `/.well-known/`. Issued automatically within seconds. Let's Encrypt issues only DV certificates. Sufficient for most websites.
- **OV (Organization Validated)**: The CA additionally verifies the organization's legal existence. Shows organization name in certificate details. Takes days to issue.
- **EV (Extended Validation)**: Rigorous multi-step identity verification — articles of incorporation, phone verification, etc. Historically showed a green address bar; modern browsers have de-emphasised the distinction.

**Certificate Transparency (CT)** is a public, append-only log of every certificate ever issued. CAs are required to log certificates before they are usable. Chrome verifies CT proofs on every certificate, making it impossible for a CA to issue a certificate for your domain without it appearing in a public, auditable log.

**The trust model's weakness**: any trusted root CA can issue a certificate for any domain. If a CA is compromised or acts maliciously, it can issue a fake certificate for `google.com` and impersonate Google to anyone who trusts that CA. **Certificate pinning** (HPKP, now deprecated) and **CT logs** exist to mitigate this. If your browser starts seeing an unexpected certificate for a popular domain, CT logs let the domain owner detect the rogue issuance quickly.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The `tls.connect()` API lets you inspect a live TLS session programmatically. `socket.authorized` is `false` if certificate verification failed — the `authorizationError` field tells you why (expired, hostname mismatch, unknown CA, etc.). When configuring an HTTPS server, `minVersion: 'TLSv1.2'` drops clients on deprecated TLS 1.0/1.1. The cipher list prefers ECDHE suites for forward secrecy; `honorCipherOrder: true` ensures the server enforces this preference even if a client advertises weak ciphers first.

sections.title: The TLS 1.3 Handshake: Step by Step
sections.content:
Now that we have the cryptographic building blocks, let us walk through exactly what happens in a TLS 1.3 handshake.

**Step 1 — ClientHello**: The client sends a `ClientHello` message containing: the TLS version it supports (TLS 1.3 clients send `0x0303` for compatibility but signal TLS 1.3 via extensions), a list of supported cipher suites (`TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384` etc.), a list of supported elliptic curves, and — critically — a `key_share` extension containing the client's ECDHE public key for its preferred curve. The client also sends a 32-byte random nonce (`client_random`).

**Step 2 — ServerHello**: The server replies in one flight with `ServerHello` (chosen cipher suite and its ECDHE public key), then immediately follows with `EncryptedExtensions`, `Certificate`, `CertificateVerify`, and `Finished` — all of these are **already encrypted** using the handshake key derived from the ECDHE exchange. This is a major TLS 1.3 improvement: in TLS 1.2, the certificate was in plaintext.

**Step 3 — Key derivation**: Both sides now independently compute the ECDHE shared secret and run it through `HKDF` (HMAC-based Key Derivation Function) with the `client_random` and `server_random` as additional entropy. HKDF produces separate keys for: handshake encryption (for the rest of the handshake), client-to-server application data, and server-to-client application data.

**Step 4 — CertificateVerify**: The server signs a hash of the entire handshake transcript so far (including the ClientHello and ServerHello) using the private key matching its certificate. This message proves the server possesses the private key — eliminating the MITM threat.

**Step 5 — Finished**: Both sides compute a `Finished` message — an HMAC over the entire handshake transcript. If either side's HMAC does not match, the handshake is aborted. This ensures neither side was tampered with during the handshake.

**Step 6 — Application data**: The client sends its `Finished` and can immediately follow with the first `GET` request in the same TLS record. Total latency: 1 RTT (plus the underlying TCP handshake).

**0-RTT (Early Data)**: TLS 1.3 optionally allows clients that have connected before to send data with zero additional round trips, using a pre-shared session ticket. However, 0-RTT data has **no forward secrecy** (it is encrypted with a key derived from the previous session's ticket) and is **replayable** (an attacker can retransmit a captured 0-RTT request). For these reasons, 0-RTT should only be used for idempotent requests (e.g., `GET`, not `POST`).

sections.title: Cipher Suites: What Changed from TLS 1.2 to TLS 1.3
sections.content:
A **cipher suite** is a named combination of algorithms used by a TLS connection. In TLS 1.2, a suite like `ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384` encodes: key exchange (ECDHE), authentication (RSA), bulk encryption (AES-256-GCM), and MAC (SHA-384). TLS 1.2 had **hundreds** of supported suites, many involving legacy algorithms that turned out to be weak: RC4 (stream cipher with statistical biases), 3DES (vulnerable to SWEET32 birthday attack), CBC mode without proper padding (POODLE, BEAST), and MD5/SHA-1 in MACs.

TLS 1.3 strips this down to **exactly five cipher suites**:
- `TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256`
- `TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384`
- `TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256`
- `TLS_AES_128_CCM_SHA256`
- `TLS_AES_128_CCM_8_SHA256`

Notice: key exchange is no longer part of the suite name. TLS 1.3 mandates ECDHE for all handshakes (or pure DHE), so it is implicit. Authentication (the certificate algorithm) is also separated. The suite only specifies the **symmetric cipher** (all are AEAD) and the **hash function for HKDF**. This simplification eliminates entire categories of attacks.

**ChaCha20-Poly1305** deserves special mention. ChaCha20 is a stream cipher designed by Daniel Bernstein that does not require hardware AES acceleration. On mobile devices and embedded systems without AES-NI instructions, ChaCha20-Poly1305 is **faster** than AES-GCM and equally secure. TLS 1.3's inclusion of it means even low-end devices get fast, strong encryption.

**Key changes in TLS 1.3 vs TLS 1.2**:
- Removed: RSA key transport (no forward secrecy), static DH, DSA, RC4, 3DES, MD5, SHA-1 in any capacity
- Removed: TLS renegotiation (source of multiple vulnerabilities)
- Removed: TLS compression (CRIME attack vector)
- Added: Mandatory forward secrecy via ephemeral DH only
- Added: Encrypted server certificate (privacy improvement)
- Added: 0-RTT mode for session resumption
- Reduced: 2 RTT handshake → 1 RTT

sections.title: OCSP, Revocation, and Certificate Lifetime
sections.content:
What happens when a certificate's private key is stolen before the certificate expires? The CA can **revoke** the certificate — marking it as invalid even before `notAfter`. Two mechanisms deliver revocation information:

**CRL (Certificate Revocation List)**: The CA periodically publishes a signed list of revoked serial numbers. Clients download the CRL and check it. CRLs can be large (megabytes for major CAs), they are only updated periodically (latency between revocation and the CRL update), and they require a network fetch per CA.

**OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol)**: A real-time protocol where the client sends a certificate serial number to the CA's OCSP responder and receives a signed `good`, `revoked`, or `unknown` response. More timely than CRL, but: (1) adds latency to every TLS handshake, (2) leaks browsing history to the CA (your OCSP query reveals which sites you visit), and (3) fails if the OCSP responder is unreachable.

**OCSP Stapling** elegantly solves both problems. The server periodically fetches its own OCSP response from the CA (e.g., every hour), caches it, and **staples** (includes) it in the TLS handshake. The response is signed by the CA, so the client can verify it without any extra round trip. The client's browsing history is not revealed to the CA. Staleness risk is bounded by the staple's validity window (typically 7 days).

**OCSP Must-Staple** is a certificate extension that instructs clients to reject the certificate if the server does not provide a valid stapled OCSP response. This closes the 'soft fail' problem — in many implementations, if OCSP is unreachable, browsers accept the certificate anyway (fail-open), defeating revocation entirely. Must-Staple turns this into fail-closed.

**Why certificates expire**: Short validity periods (90 days for Let's Encrypt) serve as a forcing function. Even if revocation fails (and it often does in practice), a stolen key is only useful for a limited window. The ACME protocol (RFC 8555) automates renewal — tools like Certbot, Caddy, and cloud load balancers renew certificates automatically before expiry, making 90-day certs operationally practical.

The error codes map directly to what Node.js, curl, and OpenSSL report — memorising even the top 4 will save hours of debugging. The HSTS checklist captures the irreversible nature of preload submission: once browsers ship with your domain in their preload list, every user worldwide is hard-coded to use HTTPS — you cannot roll it back without waiting for a browser release cycle.

sections.title: mTLS, Certificate Pinning, and Advanced Patterns
sections.content:
Standard TLS authenticates only the **server** to the client. **mTLS (mutual TLS)** adds client authentication: the client also presents a certificate, and the server verifies it. This is the standard authentication mechanism for:
- **Service-to-service communication** in microservices (service mesh tools like Istio and Linkerd implement mTLS automatically between pods)
- **Zero-trust networks** where network location is not trusted — every connection requires mutual authentication
- **API clients** where you want to restrict access to specific known clients without passwords

In mTLS, after the server sends `CertificateVerify`, it sends a `CertificateRequest` message, and the client responds with its own `Certificate` and `CertificateVerify`. The server validates the client certificate against a CA it trusts (often an internal CA).

**Certificate Pinning** was an attempt to solve the 'any CA can vouch for any domain' problem. An app or configuration could pin a specific certificate's public key — refusing connections unless the server presents a cert with that exact key. HTTP Public Key Pinning (HPKP) was a browser feature that allowed websites to declare their pins via an HTTP header. It was removed from browsers in 2018 after widespread misconfiguration permanently broke access to sites. Today, **Certificate Transparency** serves a similar accountability purpose without the operational danger.

**SNI (Server Name Indication)** is a TLS extension where the client sends the hostname in `ClientHello` (in plaintext). This allows a single server with one IP address to serve multiple domains with different certificates — the server reads the hostname and loads the correct certificate before responding. Without SNI, HTTPS required one IP per domain. SNI is nearly universal today, but the hostname is visible to network observers — **Encrypted Client Hello (ECH)**, still being standardised, aims to encrypt this extension.

**TLS Termination at load balancers**: In most production deployments, the browser's TLS session terminates at the load balancer (Nginx, HAProxy, AWS ALB, Cloudflare). Traffic from the load balancer to backend servers may travel over a private network as plain HTTP, or may be re-encrypted with a second TLS session using an internal certificate. The first model is faster but requires trusting the internal network; the second (end-to-end TLS or mTLS) is preferred in high-security environments.

flowchart LR
    B["Browser"] -- "TLS (public cert)" --> LB["Load Balancer\n(TLS termination)"]
    LB -- "HTTP or mTLS" --> S1["Service A"]
    LB -- "HTTP or mTLS" --> S2["Service B"]
    S1 -- "mTLS" --> S3["Service C"]
    S2 -- "mTLS" --> S3
sections.caption: Common production TLS topology: browser TLS terminates at the load balancer; internal services communicate over plain HTTP or mTLS depending on the security model.

sections.title: Common Mistakes, Misconfigurations, and Debugging
sections.content:
**Incomplete certificate chain**: The most common server misconfiguration. A server must send the leaf certificate plus every intermediate certificate between the leaf and the trusted root. Browsers can sometimes fetch missing intermediates via the `Authority Information Access` extension, but this adds latency and is unreliable. Test with: `openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -showcerts` and verify the full chain appears.

**Expired certificates in production**: Automation solves this. Let's Encrypt + Certbot (or Caddy's built-in ACME) renews certificates automatically. Set monitoring that alerts at 30 days and again at 7 days. The root cause of most expiry outages is a manual certificate that someone forgot to renew.

**TLS 1.0/1.1 still enabled**: Both versions were deprecated in 2021 (RFC 8996). PCI-DSS compliance requires disabling them. Set `minVersion: 'TLSv1.2'` in Node.js, `ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3` in Nginx.

**Weak cipher suites**: Cipher suites without ECDHE or DHE prefix (e.g., plain `RSA-AES256-CBC-SHA`) provide no forward secrecy. Suites using CBC mode are vulnerable to padding oracle attacks unless implemented with strict constant-time MAC-then-decrypt (and almost nothing is). Remove all non-ECDHE and non-AEAD suites.

**Missing HSTS header**: Without `Strict-Transport-Security`, a user who types `http://example.com` makes an unprotected request before being redirected to HTTPS — an SSL-strip attack intercepts this. The HSTS header instructs the browser to always use HTTPS for the domain for `max-age` seconds, even before any response is received (after the first compliant response).

**Self-signed certificates in production**: Seen frequently in internal services. They cause all client libraries to fail by default. Use a private CA (e.g., `step-ca`, AWS Private CA) to issue internal certificates — clients can be configured to trust the private root CA without resorting to `rejectUnauthorized: false` (which disables all TLS security).

**Debugging tools**: `openssl s_client -connect host:443` shows the full handshake, cert chain, and cipher negotiated. `ssllabs.com/ssltest` grades your server's TLS configuration and lists every vulnerability. `curl -v https://host` shows certificate details. `tls.connect()` in Node.js gives programmatic access to all negotiated parameters.

**Historical context**: SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) was invented by Netscape in 1994 for the early web. SSL 2.0 (1995) had critical flaws; SSL 3.0 (1996) was better but still vulnerable to POODLE (2014). TLS 1.0 (1999) was essentially SSL 3.1 — renamed to distance it from SSL's reputation. TLS 1.1 (2006) added protection against CBC attacks. TLS 1.2 (2008) added AEAD cipher suites and SHA-2. TLS 1.3 (2018) was a clean break: it took 4 years of IETF debate, 28 draft versions, and went through controversy (the NSA pushed for a 'static DH' mode that would have enabled lawful interception — the IETF rejected it). The result is the most thoroughly analysed cryptographic protocol ever standardised.

**Interview and production traps**: (1) 'Forward secrecy means past sessions are safe even if the server's private key is later stolen' — know exactly why (ephemeral ECDHE keys discarded after handshake). (2) The server's certificate proves identity in `CertificateVerify` — a signature over the handshake transcript, not just the key exchange. (3) `UNABLE_TO_VERIFY_LEAF_SIGNATURE` almost always means the server is not sending intermediate certs, not that the cert is invalid. (4) Setting `rejectUnauthorized: false` in Node.js disables all TLS verification — never use it in production, even for internal services; use a private CA instead. (5) `0-RTT` data is replayable — safe for `GET`, dangerous for `POST /payment`. (6) Run `ssllabs.com/ssltest` on your domain before your next security review — it catches weak ciphers, incomplete chains, and missing HSTS in seconds.

items: **TLS combines asymmetric and symmetric cryptography**: ECDHE during the handshake to securely establish a shared secret, then fast AEAD symmetric encryption (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) for all application data.

**TLS 1.3 handshake completes in 1 RTT**: `ClientHello` carries the ECDHE public key; `ServerHello` carries the server's ECDHE key plus an already-encrypted `Certificate`, `CertificateVerify`, and `Finished`. Session keys are derived independently by both sides from the ECDHE shared secret via HKDF.

**Forward secrecy is mandatory in TLS 1.3**: Fresh ephemeral ECDHE key pairs are generated and discarded every handshake. Even a full compromise of the server's long-term private key cannot decrypt past sessions, because the ephemeral keys that derived the session keys no longer exist.

**X.509 certificates bind a public key to an identity** and are signed by a Certificate Authority. Browsers verify: (1) the full chain of signatures to a trusted root CA, (2) the domain matches a Subject Alternative Name, (3) the validity period, and (4) the certificate is not revoked (OCSP/CRL).

**PKI trust is transitive**: browsers pre-install ~150 root CA certificates. Any of these CAs can sign any domain's certificate. Certificate Transparency (CT) logs every issued certificate publicly, making rogue issuance detectable even if a CA misbehaves.

**OCSP stapling** eliminates the revocation latency and privacy problem: the server fetches and caches its own signed OCSP response and includes it in the handshake, so the client gets revocation proof with zero additional round trips.

**mTLS** extends standard TLS to authenticate both parties — the client presents a certificate in addition to the server. This is the standard pattern for zero-trust service-to-service communication in modern microservice architectures.

quiz.question: In a TLS 1.3 full handshake, how many round trips are required before the client can send application data?
options: 0 RTT
1 RTT
2 RTT
3 RTT
quiz.explanation: TLS 1.3 requires exactly 1 RTT. The client sends ClientHello (with ECDHE key_share) in the first flight. The server responds with ServerHello, Certificate, CertificateVerify, and Finished in one flight. The client sends its Finished and can immediately append application data — making the total 1 RTT for the TLS layer (plus 1 RTT for the underlying TCP handshake). TLS 1.2 required 2 RTTs.

quiz.question: Why does TLS 1.3 mandate forward secrecy while TLS 1.2 only made it optional?
options: TLS 1.3 uses longer RSA keys, which are inherently forward-secret
TLS 1.3 removed RSA key transport and requires ephemeral ECDHE for all key exchanges
Forward secrecy was patented and only became freely available in 2018
TLS 1.2 achieved forward secrecy through certificate pinning
quiz.explanation: In TLS 1.2, suites like RSA-AES256-CBC-SHA performed 'RSA key transport' — the client encrypted a random pre-master secret with the server's RSA public key. If an attacker recorded traffic and later obtained the server's RSA private key, they could decrypt the pre-master secret and derive all session keys. TLS 1.3 removed these suites entirely, requiring ephemeral ECDHE for every handshake, making forward secrecy mandatory.

quiz.question: What does the CertificateVerify message prove in a TLS 1.3 handshake?
options: That the certificate has not expired
That the CA has confirmed the server's identity in real time
That the server possesses the private key matching the certificate's public key
That the OCSP responder has confirmed the certificate is not revoked
quiz.explanation: CertificateVerify contains a digital signature over the entire handshake transcript (all messages exchanged so far) made with the server's private key. The client verifies this signature using the server's public key (from the Certificate message). This proves the server controls the private key — eliminating man-in-the-middle attacks where an impersonator could relay a certificate they do not own.

quiz.question: In ECDHE key exchange, what exactly is discarded after the handshake to achieve forward secrecy?
options: The server's long-term certificate private key
The symmetric session keys used for application data
The ephemeral per-session ECDHE private keys (a and b)
The HKDF output used to derive the session keys
quiz.explanation: Both the client (private key 'a') and server (private key 'b') generate fresh ephemeral ECDHE key pairs for every handshake and discard them immediately after key derivation. The session keys are derived solely from the ECDHE shared secret. An attacker who records all traffic and later steals the server's long-term certificate private key cannot recompute 'a' or 'b', so they cannot derive the session keys for any past session.

quiz.question: What field in an X.509 certificate does a browser use to verify the hostname of a TLS connection?
options: The Common Name (CN) field in the Subject
The Subject Alternative Names (SAN) extension
The Issuer's Organization (O) field
The certificate's Serial Number
quiz.explanation: Modern browsers use the Subject Alternative Names (SAN) extension, which lists all hostnames and IP addresses the certificate is valid for. The old CN (Common Name) field is no longer consulted for hostname verification by modern browsers and TLS libraries. A certificate can cover multiple domains via SAN (multi-SAN cert) or use a wildcard like *.example.com to cover one subdomain level.

quiz.question: What is the primary advantage of OCSP Stapling over standard OCSP?
options: It permanently pins the certificate, preventing future revocation
The server fetches and attaches the CA's signed OCSP response to the handshake, eliminating a separate client request
It compresses the certificate chain to reduce handshake overhead
The client caches OCSP responses indefinitely for faster future connections
quiz.explanation: Without stapling, the client must make a separate HTTP request to the CA's OCSP responder during every TLS handshake, adding latency and revealing which websites the client visits to the CA. With OCSP stapling, the server periodically fetches and caches the CA-signed OCSP response, then attaches it to the TLS handshake. The client verifies the CA signature on the stapled response with no extra round trip and no privacy leak.

quiz.question: How many cipher suites does TLS 1.3 support, and what property do they all share?
options: Hundreds, to maintain backwards compatibility with TLS 1.2 clients
Exactly 5, and all use AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data)
Exactly 3, and all use RSA for key exchange
Exactly 10, and all support both CBC and GCM modes
quiz.explanation: TLS 1.3 defines exactly 5 cipher suites: TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, TLS_AES_128_CCM_SHA256, and TLS_AES_128_CCM_8_SHA256. All are AEAD algorithms — they provide confidentiality and integrity in a single operation. Key exchange (always ECDHE) is no longer encoded in the suite name. TLS 1.2 had hundreds of suites, many with weak algorithms like RC4, 3DES, and CBC without AEAD.

quiz.question: What TLS error most likely indicates the server is not sending its intermediate certificate(s)?
options: ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID
ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID
UNABLE_TO_VERIFY_LEAF_SIGNATURE
ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID
quiz.explanation: UNABLE_TO_VERIFY_LEAF_SIGNATURE means the client cannot verify the signature on the leaf certificate because it does not have the intermediate CA's public key. This happens when the server sends only the leaf cert without the intermediate certs that bridge to a trusted root. ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID means the root CA is not trusted. ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID means the cert is expired or not yet valid.

quiz.question: In the context of TLS 1.3, why is 0-RTT (Early Data) considered risky for POST requests?
options: POST requests are too large to fit in the first TLS record
0-RTT data is encrypted without forward secrecy and can be replayed by an attacker
POST requests are rejected by the server until the Finished message is verified
0-RTT only supports GET and HEAD methods by protocol definition
quiz.explanation: 0-RTT data is encrypted using a key derived from a session ticket from a previous connection — it has no forward secrecy (unlike regular TLS 1.3 sessions). More critically, 0-RTT data is replayable: an attacker who captures the 0-RTT record can resend it to the server, causing the server to process the request twice. For idempotent GET requests this is acceptable, but for POST /payment or POST /order, a replay could create duplicate transactions.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) preload list?
options: It preloads the server's TLS certificate into the browser cache for faster handshakes
It allows browsers to hard-code domains as HTTPS-only, preventing any initial HTTP request that could be SSL-stripped
It requires the CA to preload OCSP responses before issuing a certificate
It preloads approved cipher suites into the browser to speed up negotiation
quiz.explanation: The HSTS header instructs browsers to always use HTTPS after the first compliant response — but an SSL-stripping attacker can intercept that very first HTTP request before the header is seen. The HSTS preload list (hstspreload.org) ships domains hard-coded as HTTPS-only inside the browser binary itself, so even the very first-ever visit goes directly to HTTPS with no HTTP request that could be intercepted. This is permanent and requires all subdomains to also support HTTPS.
